How a catalogue is kept

A catalogue is a promise that a book can be found. Every title that enters the building is given a place on a shelf and a line in a list, and the two must agree for as long as the book stays. When they stop agreeing, the book is as good as lost, although it has not moved an inch.

The work begins at the door. A new book is opened, its title page is read, and its author, title and year are written down exactly as they are printed. Nothing is corrected at this stage. A name that is spelled in three ways by three publishers is recorded in three ways, and joined later under one heading.

Subjects are harder than names. Two readers who want the same book will ask for it in different words, and the catalogue has to answer both. For this reason every subject has one chosen term, and the other terms point to it. The pointing costs time, but it is what makes a search end at the right shelf.

Shelves fill up, and books move. Each move is written into the list on the same day, by the person who carried the book. A move that waits until tomorrow is often forgotten, and a forgotten move is found only when a reader comes back from the shelf with empty hands.

Once a year the list is read against the shelves. Two people walk the rooms, one reading the list aloud and the other touching each spine. They note what is missing, what has been found, and what stands in the wrong place. The count takes a week and is the dullest work of the year.

None of this is visible to the reader, and that is the point. A good catalogue is noticed only when it fails. On every other day it is simply the reason that a question asked at the desk is answered in a minute.
